1.pericope_label: Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?
debates: Whether the word means the fat or the milk
Whether the shepherds are the civil rulers or the priests
Where the blame for the scattering falls
outliers: Gill and Clarke report that fat and milk differ only in the pointing and that several ancient versions read milk, which Clarke prefers
Gill and Clarke both take the shepherds to include civil and ecclesiastical rulers alike, while Ellicott holds the term is used of rulers and distinguished elsewhere from prophets and priests
Ellicott lays the calamities at the door of the rulers, not because the people were sinless but because their sins were largely due to the example of those over them
Keil and Delitzsch head the chapter as the opening of the promise of salvation that runs through the following chapters
themes: One Greek word serving both for feeding sheep and for governing people
A broken bone splinted until it knits
A shepherd who counts his flock often enough that no stray gets far
Dignity and power that do not exempt from reproof

7.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord God, Behold, I am against the shepherds; and I will require my flock at their hand, and cause them to cease from feeding the flock
debates: What the penalty on the shepherds consists of
Whether the sentence has been enacted since
outliers: Gill takes the repeated summons as confirmation and as leaving the shepherds inexcusable
Henry holds that the name and authority of a shepherd will not engage God for one who does not do the work enjoined him
Henry distinguishes two penalties, an accounting for the missing flock and deprivation of both the work and the wages
Clarke reads the sentence as already enacted in his own country, where a hierarchy was unpriested and a better qualified set raised up
themes: A flock lost twice over, to deceivers and then to destroyers
A doom read to those who would not hear a direction
A warning to the successors of deposed shepherds
The character of a bad shepherd left to be inferred by reversal

11.pericope_label: For thus saith the Lord God, Behold, I, even I, will both search my sheep, and seek them out
debates: Whether the promises are earthly or spiritual
outliers: Ellicott holds that the whole chain of promises is contained in the assurance that the Lord himself will be the shepherd, and must be understood spiritually
Ellicott assigns a layered fulfilment, partly in the return from exile and partly under the Maccabees, both types of a greater deliverance
Gill likewise stages the fulfilment, in the end of the captivity and then in a later gathering from all countries
Ellicott denies that feeding with judgment means with wisdom, and reads it as with righteousness and authority
themes: Earthly language said to be the only vehicle for a promise otherwise inconceivable
Fatness read as the prosperity that begets hardness of heart
Milk for babes and meat for strong men
A flock counted over after the scattering

17.pericope_label: And as for you, O my flock, thus saith the Lord God; Behold, I judge between cattle and cattle, between the rams and the he goats
debates: Whether the judgment is between classes of the flock or within each class
Who the rams and he-goats are
What the trampling and fouling stand for
outliers: Ellicott holds the judgment is not between the cattle and the rams but within each class, so that all the evil of whatever rank are rejected
Wesley takes the rams for rulers, Clarke for false professors, Henry for the rich who bear hard on their poor neighbours
Ellicott sums the charge as supplying themselves first and then with careless insolence destroying what should have been left for others
Henry suspects the rams and he-goats also stand for a later party of teachers who devoured the houses of widows
themes: Sheep observed to shelter a sick one from the heat of the sun
Sporting dogs fed before the poor at the door
The weakest going to the wall
Water muddied so that what is left is embittered

23.pericope_label: And I will set up one shepherd over them, and he shall feed them, even my servant David; he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd
debates: Whether David here is the person or a type
Whether the promises of this section are literal or spiritual
What the plant of renown is
outliers: Ellicott argues that a literal reading of the restoration would require the governor to be David himself, and takes the absurdity of that as evidence the whole is spiritual
Ellicott holds the shepherd is one against the many evil rulers before him and against the two kingdoms to be united, so that no merely human ruler can fulfil it
Clarke allows the plant of renown might be a community of believers but thinks it more probably one person, elsewhere called a branch and a rod
Gill rejects the reading of one authority who made the plant the Jewish nation itself
themes: A covenant cut, with the halves laid opposite and the parties meeting between them
A consistency test applied to literal reading
A last verse used by the rabbis to argue who may be called men
The centre of the old order made the centre from which the new goes out
